theme: My heart is steadfast, O God
readingInstruction: Read Psalm 108. It is a psalm made of two earlier psalms, joined together. Notice the confident praise at the beginning and the honest need at the end.
settingTheScene: Psalm 108 is a psalm of David, made from parts of two other psalms: verses 1 to 5 are almost identical to Psalm 57:7-11, and verses 6 to 13 are almost identical to Psalm 60:5-12. This was used in worship as a song for a nation facing enemies and hoping for God’s help. It is a fitting prayer after the fall of Jerusalem, since it begins with praise and ends with trust in God alone when human help fails.
observation: “My heart is steadfast, O God! I will sing and make melody with all my being!” (v. 1).
“Awake, O harp and lyre! I will awake the dawn!” (v. 2).
“I will give thanks to you, O LORD, among the peoples” (v. 3).
“For your steadfast love is great above the heavens; your faithfulness reaches to the clouds” (v. 4).
“Be exalted, O God, above the heavens! Let your glory be over all the earth!” (v. 5).
“That your beloved ones may be delivered, give salvation by your right hand and answer me!” (v. 6).
“Have you not rejected us, O God? You do not go out, O God, with our armies” (v. 11).
“Through God we will do valiantly; it is he who will tread down our foes” (v. 13).
interpretation:
The psalm begins with a vow. “My heart is steadfast.” The word means firm, fixed, established. Whatever is happening around him, his heart is anchored in God. And the result is song, with all his being. He even says he will wake the dawn, rather than waiting for morning to wake him. His praise is not tied to circumstances.

The praise then widens to include the nations: “among the peoples… among the nations.” God’s steadfast love is above the heavens, and so his praise must be heard everywhere. The psalmist’s confidence rests on God’s character. Notice the two terms again: steadfast love and faithfulness. They are the pillars of God’s covenant.

Then the psalm shifts to prayer and to a series of divine promises. God has spoken in his holiness: he will divide Shechem, measure the Valley of Succoth, and claim Gilead, Manasseh, Ephraim, and Judah. Moab is his washbasin, Edom his slave. These are the promises of the land, spoken to David. God will give victory.

But the last part is honest. “Who will lead me to the fortified city? Who will lead me to Edom? Have you not rejected us, O God?” The psalmist admits that the people are in trouble, that God does not seem to be going out with their armies. He pleads: “Oh grant us help against the foe, for vain is the salvation of man!” Human help fails. “Through God we will do valiantly.” The psalm ends with a statement of faith in the middle of weakness.

This is a good prayer for the exile and for every believer who is both confident and needy. We can praise the God whose love is above the heavens even as we ask for help in a world where our own strength fails.
connection: Psalm 108’s praise among the nations is picked up in Romans 15:9-11. Ephesians 3:20 says God is able to do far more abundantly than all that we ask or think. Philippians 4:13 says, “I can do all things through him who strengthens me.” Psalm 20:7 says some trust in chariots, but we trust in the name of the LORD. John 15:5 says that apart from Christ we can do nothing.
application:
Start tomorrow morning with the vow of verse 2: “I will awake the dawn.” Sing or pray aloud before anything else.

Trust God, not human help, in an area where you have been leaning on your own plans.

Praise the LORD among someone who does not know him, by telling them one thing he has done.
prayerPrompts: Tell God your heart is steadfast, or ask him to make it so.
Sing or speak your praise to him in your own words.
Ask him to be exalted above the heavens.
